title: The 2026 Am Law 100 Power Rankings — Jae Um
pub: AAA — AI and the Future of Law (YouTube)
author: Jae Um

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Practitioner engagement: Redesign should precede technological certainty
st.an: The excerpt only describes the scope and compressed production process of Um’s power rankings. Although it introduces a forthcoming AI anecdote, it provides no account of AI use or view on practitioner-led experimentation, implementation, reliability, governance, access to justice or professional redesign.

st.t: Agentic infrastructure: Harvey tests vertical vendor durability
st.an: Um accepts the cluster’s operating-model premise and materially extends its buyer-side implications through “bionic insourcing.” She argues that AI should prompt firms to stress-test vulnerabilities and legal departments to reallocate work according to business-process integration and proximity to legal judgment, while cautioning that insourcing is not categorically preferable.
qs: What are our vulnerabilities?—I think that kind of critical examination of your business model is really important in disruption cycles.

So I think what AI raises—the questions that AI raises that are of great interest here—and I tried to label that one, I think I labeled it “bionic insourcing.”  When you guys talk about bionic boutiques, I hope you tack this on, because it is the other side.

st.t: Legal economics: AI makes adoption a model problem
st.an: Um accepts that AI-driven competition requires strategic adaptation rather than simple tool deployment. She materially extends the cluster by proposing immersive first-year training as a way to discover scalable applications and by identifying AI-enabled entry into new market segments as a possible business-model opportunity, while treating outcomes as prospective.
qs: And it’s only by immersing people in it that firms will find scalable applications.
So it’s not just about training—it may open up a different segment of the market.

st.t: Operating model: AI shifts bargaining across providers
st.an: Um accepts the operating-model framing and materially develops it through “bionic insourcing”: reallocating work according to proximity to business processes and legal judgment rather than simply shifting it to firms or ALSPs. She also adds a concrete talent model—immersive first-year AI training to identify scalable applications—while treating market expansion and value at scale as possibilities rather than established outcomes.
qs: But there’s also way more work that’s going out to firms or even ALSPs that would be better done differently inside, because of the embedding with business processes, or the proximity required to apply legal judgment quickly.
And it’s only by immersing people in it that firms will find scalable applications.

st.t: Production model: Institutional absorption governs AI value
st.an: The source accepts that AI value depends on organisational and business-model redesign rather than investment alone, and materially extends the cluster with concrete proposals: immersive junior training to discover scalable applications, strategic testing of firm vulnerabilities, and reallocating work according to business-process integration and proximity to legal judgment. Its caution about limited value at scale also reinforces the cluster’s qualification of ambitious forecasts.
qs: What are our vulnerabilities?—I think that kind of critical examination of your business model is really important in disruption cycles.

But there’s also way more work that’s going out to firms or even ALSPs that would be better done differently inside, because of the embedding with business processes, or the proximity required to apply legal judgment quickly.

st.t: Service model: AI challenges production more than lawyers
st.an: Um accepts that AI will restructure legal-service production and competitive economics rather than eliminate the profession. She materially extends the cluster by tying workflow investment to each firm’s competitive strategy and arguing that AI-enabled in-house insourcing may reallocate work more radically than AI-enabled boutiques.
qs: What I’m trying to show with these examples is that you can’t have an AI strategy that’s separate from your competitive strategy.

But there’s also way more work that’s going out to firms or even ALSPs that would be better done differently inside, because of the embedding with business processes, or the proximity required to apply legal judgment quickly.

st.t: Service redesign: Resistance reflects incentives and identity
st.an: Um accepts the cluster’s organisational-change framing and materially develops it by tying AI investment to each firm’s competitive strategy, leadership trust, capital constraints, protected experimentation and work allocation. Her firm examples and proposals add concrete strategic mechanisms, while remaining largely experiential and predictive rather than demonstrating returns.
qs: What I’m trying to show with these examples is that you can’t have an AI strategy that’s separate from your competitive strategy.
They’re allowing associates to count up to 400 hours of AI experimentation toward their billable targets.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Um accepts the cluster’s core view that AI creates substantial task-level gains only when paired with suitable data, user direction and workflow redesign. She materially extends it with a firsthand analytical-workflow example and a strategic account of firm-specific investment, AI-enabled insourcing and gradual demand erosion, while treating market-wide disruption as a prediction rather than an established outcome.
qs: You do have to work with it—you need a clean data structure, a good data dictionary, and clear communication.
Because it’s not just buying tools—you have to try them, integrate them, change workflows.

st.t: Workflow unbundling: Buyers challenge time-based production
st.an: Um accepts the cluster’s expectation of intensifying competition from emerging substitutes and differentiated market segments, while extending it with evidence of profit concentration and forecasts of consolidation and refragmentation among incumbent firms. Her view also reinforces the cluster’s caution that disruption implies turbulence and adaptation, not the profession’s imminent displacement, though she does not directly address buyer-led workflow unbundling, pricing reform, training or verification.
qs: So I think what we’re seeing is a classic disruptive cycle, where incumbents face increasing competitive intensity among each other, and invisible pressure from substitutes they can’t see the whites of the eyes of yet—Norm AI, General Legal, all of these things that are popping up, and all the money going into them.

st.t: Associate training: Automation threatens expertise reproduction
st.an: Um supports the cluster’s call for deliberate, funded adaptation of associate training by endorsing protected experimentation time and intensive first-year AI training. Her focus is on AI immersion and workflow innovation rather than directly establishing the cluster’s central claim that automation erodes the experience needed for independent judgment and verification.
qs: They’re allowing associates to count up to 400 hours of AI experimentation toward their billable targets.
One of the proposals I floated a few years ago was that a firm could draw a line and say, we’re not going to charge for first years—we’re going to train them intensively on AI.

st.t: Delivery economics: AI pressures pricing and apprenticeship
st.an: Um aligns with the cluster’s account that AI pressures legal-delivery economics through client-driven work reallocation, workflow change, billable-hour pressure and competitive restructuring. She also supports the view that implementation requires strategic alignment, protected lawyer time and integration rather than mere tool access, while treating market-wide outcomes and returns as still uncertain.
qs: What I’m trying to show with these examples is that you can’t have an AI strategy that’s separate from your competitive strategy.

But there’s also way more work that’s going out to firms or even ALSPs that would be better done differently inside, because of the embedding with business processes, or the proximity required to apply legal judgment quickly.

kp.k: AI enables analyst-directed data processing and scenario testing
kp.d: Um describes using Claude for her 2026 rankings, covering 100 firms and about 55 component measures combined into composite KPIs. Previously, data shaping and base calculations alone took about three full days. This year she reports speaking instructions rather than typing formulas, testing alternative KPI weightings simultaneously, and directing visualizations. This is a personal workflow account, conditional on initial capability setup, clean data structures, a data dictionary and clear communication; she says she would not have trusted the previous year's technology with the compressed project.
qs: This year, I did not type a single formula. I spoke the analytics into being.
Once I had the KPIs designed, I could run multiple scenarios—different weightings—simultaneously.
You do have to work with it—you need a clean data structure, a good data dictionary, and clear communication.

kp.k: Elite firms increasingly concentrate profits and reshape competition
kp.d: Drawing on her ALM-based analysis, Um reports that six firms she labels 'apex predators' hold 24% of market share and 24% of the profit pool, compared with 16% for those firms ten years earlier in her discussion of profit concentration. She emphasizes their sustained simultaneous revenue and margin growth. She argues that this concentration changes competitors' conceptions of partnership, firm size, staffing shape and leverage; she does not attribute these observed developments solely to AI.
qs: They have 24% of market share. They have 24% of the profit pool share.
Ten years ago, those same firms had 16%.
It is changing how the rest of the market looks at the title of partner, the structure of the partnership model, the size and shape of the firm, how leveraged it needs to be.

kp.k: Policy volatility generated demand firms captured unevenly
kp.d: Um says her hypothesis 13 months earlier—that the new administration's decisions would increase corporate clients' need for lawyers—proved true. She distinguishes novel problems requiring original legal thinking from familiar problems expanding in volume. In her interpretation of quantitative results and qualitative research, differences in forecasting capacity and competing for this demand helped make the year a turning point for the Am Law 100.
qs: The hypothesis—even 13 months ago—was that the new administration was going to make decisions and take actions that would require corporate clients to need more lawyers. I think that proved to be true.
And the way certain segments of firms forecasted capacity into that demand and competed to capture it—that does show up in the numbers.

kp.k: Headcount strategies distinguish elite competitive groups
kp.d: Um identifies revenue per lawyer as the most informative metric across her five years of rankings, while stressing its dependence on headcount decisions. Her three brackets distinguish continually investing apex predators, six prestigious 'dynasty brands' that expand in strategically targeted spurts, and an 'Elite Eight' with earlier-stage strategies or narrower specializations. This is a classification of competitive growth patterns, not evidence of AI-driven staffing reductions.
qs: What drove the bracketing this year is very discernible differences in the pace and style of headcount growth.
They’ve been top of market for a long time, but you don’t stay there just by being old and fancy.
The Elite Eight, I think, are either earlier in their strategic build or still defining it.

kp.k: Client understanding matters more than management titles
kp.d: Um argues that formal corporate management structures do not necessarily predict outperformance: some dynasty firms lack a COO yet perform strongly. Chief AI officer and pricing talent pools are thin, and less formal structures can hinder recruitment, but strong client relationships and financial resources allow advantaged firms to invest when needed. She cites Davis Polk's financial-sector position and Kirkland & Ellis hiring its first COO from Blackstone as examples of different approaches.
qs: Just because a firm has a very corporate structure with lots of chiefs and clear functions does not mean they outperform.
That can make it harder to compete for top-of-market business talent—like a chief AI officer or head of pricing—because those talent pools are very thin, and demand far exceeds supply.
But the thread across the top-performing firms is not just structure—it’s that they are deeply attuned to the needs of their clients.

kp.k: Strategic clarity, partnership trust and capital enable investment
kp.d: Um recommends defining a firm's economic role and client proposition rather than treating current market position as destiny. She argues that leadership trust and optimism create room for experimentation, while limited capital, low profits and high cost per equity partner constrain risk-taking through dependence on cash flow and debt. She links these constraints to growing interest in outside investment, without discussing particular regulatory changes.
qs: Even if a firm feels like it’s on the back foot, what the power rankings show this year is that position is not destiny.
If the managing partner and leadership have earned and maintained trust with the partnership, they have much more room to explore and invest.
Some firms are simply too constrained to invest.

kp.k: AI investment includes scarce lawyer time and workflow change
kp.d: Um describes lawyer time as perishable inventory and emphasizes the opportunity cost of learning different ways to work. She reports hearing that some firms spend up to 2% of revenue on AI, without supplying a sample or audited expenditure data. The investment encompasses experimentation, integration and workflow change, not merely software purchases.
qs: The core inventory of a law firm is lawyer time.
If you want to change behavior, people have to spend time and effort working differently. That’s a real cost.
I’m hearing some firms say up to 2% of revenue, which is significant.
AI is more like a utility than a tool. You have to actually do something with it.

kp.k: AI strategies must match firms' competitive advantages
kp.d: Um presents differing investment approaches rather than proven winners: Kirkland and Cooley's quiet, serious investment; HSF Kramer's forward-deployed engineers embedded in work, fitting disputes and arbitration teams; and A&O Shearman's application-layer experience and financial-institution relationships. She argues that AI strategy should be inseparable from competitive strategy and explicitly says it is too early to grade these theses.
qs: Well, it’s early to be grading the theses.
The forward-deployed engineer model—embedding technical capability into how the work gets done—that’s interesting.
What I’m trying to show with these examples is that you can’t have an AI strategy that’s separate from your competitive strategy.
We’re not going to know immediately what’s smart and what’s not.

kp.k: Crediting AI experimentation may transform training and market reach
kp.d: Leonard reports that Ropes and Gray allows associates up to 400 hours of AI experimentation toward billable targets. Um endorses the policy, predicting returns from training relatively less productive first years, discovering scalable applications and differentiating recruitment. She distinguishes this from her earlier proposal not to charge for first years while training them intensively in AI. She also reports Julie Jones's suggestion that AI could make previously unsuitable middle-market work viable; these benefits are expectations rather than demonstrated outcomes.
qs: They’re allowing associates to count up to 400 hours of AI experimentation toward their billable targets.
From an economic standpoint, I think the ROI is going to be there.
And it’s only by immersing people in it that firms will find scalable applications.
Julie Jones said that AI could enable them to take on certain middle-market work that didn’t previously fit their model.

kp.k: Investment scale contrasts with uncertain realized AI value
kp.d: McCormack frames the leadership dilemma using $380 billion in Big Tech capex in 2025, described as 2.1 times combined Am Law 100 revenue, and a McKinsey claim that only 5% of companies obtain AI value at scale. These are host-reported figures, without underlying study details here. Um responds that public perceptions of managing partners' thinking are speculative, recommends grounding decisions in what clients buy, and insists leaders must articulate a position by the end of 2026.
qs: the capex spending from Big Tech in 2025, I think you said, was $380 billion, which is 2.1 times the Am Law 100 combined revenue
McKinsey says only 5% of companies are getting AI value at scale
By the end of 2026, the only wrong answer is saying nothing.
It becomes: I know my business—now show me what AI can do to it.

kp.k: Client substitution could silently eliminate law-firm demand
kp.d: Um uses anonymous in-house accounts to describe a scenario where clients adopt much cheaper substitutes without notifying their firms. She explicitly qualifies the interviewees as very early adopters unrepresentative of most buyers, not evidence of imminent widespread collapse. McCormack recounts one GC completing a $10,000 project with a $20-a-month tool. Um sees especially high exposure in similar work sold across dispersed clients without stable, continuing relationships, and recommends close strategic-account relationships and monitoring price-sensitive work.
qs: I think in some practices, the phone just stops ringing, and the law firm does not know why.
the quotes came from very early adopter clients who are not representative of most of the buy side.
one of your quotes was a GC who did a $10,000 project with a $20-a-month tool.
That’s the kind of market where, if a new offering comes in, the rate of adoption and diffusion will be fast, and the early signals will not be visible to law firms.

kp.k: Bionic insourcing could fundamentally reconfigure corporate legal work
kp.d: Um argues that sourcing should follow the optimal way to perform work, including proximity to business processes and the need for rapid legal judgment. While disagreeing with some insourcing over the previous ten years, she believes more work currently sent to firms or ALSPs would be better performed internally in different ways. She predicts AI-enabled 'bionic insourcing' could depart more radically from existing legal departments than AI-enabled boutiques depart from conventional firms, and recommends adversarial examination of incumbent business models.
qs: But there’s also way more work that’s going out to firms or even ALSPs that would be better done differently inside, because of the embedding with business processes, or the proximity required to apply legal judgment quickly.
I think bionic boutiques will just be supercharged law firms, but bionic insourcing could look like a completely different thing.
that kind of critical examination of your business model is really important in disruption cycles.

kp.k: Clients may force cannibalization of inefficient billable hours
kp.d: Leonard quotes an anonymous corporate counsel demanding that firms eliminate inefficient hours or lose work to competitors. Um interprets this as a possible mechanism for AI's effects to appear indirectly: fewer new matters, more difficulty winning business and obtaining rates, and slipping realization, rather than a clearly attributable AI failure event. This is her forecast of market pressure, not a reported measured decline.
qs: If a firm isn’t cannibalizing its own inefficient billable hours, we will find a firm that will.
You’re going to see your inventory—your new matters—tick down. It’s going to be harder to get rates. Realization is going to slip. And it’s going to be hard to say why.

kp.k: Disruption may combine incumbent consolidation and new challengers
kp.d: Um recalls estimating three years earlier that roughly 300 consequential global firms served enterprise clients and were intended to outlast their name partners. She doubts there is room for the current set, partly because she questions whether enough management teams can navigate the transition. She predicts consolidation, 'refragmentation', competition among industrial-scale firms and pressure from emerging substitutes such as Norm AI and General Legal backed by venture capital and private equity. She expressly predicts survival of the profession, not its disappearance, alongside larger gains for winners.
qs: I don’t believe there’s room for the current set of 300.
I think there will be a refragmentation. I think there will be a clash of the titans in these industrial-scale firms.

incumbents face increasing competitive intensity among each other, and invisible pressure from substitutes they can’t see the whites of the eyes of yet—Norm AI, General Legal, all of these things that are popping up, and all the money going into them.
the profession has survived every previous wave of disruption. It will survive this one too.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Jae Um reports that AI substantially changed how she produced legal-market analytics, replacing hands-on formula writing and data manipulation with directed analysis.
pts.d: For the 2026 power rankings, Um says she used Claude to perform calculations, test multiple KPI weightings simultaneously, examine sensitivity, and produce directed visualizations. Her evidence is personal experience with a recurring project involving 100 firms and roughly 55 component measures, not a controlled productivity study. She describes the system as an on-demand analytical team that reduces handoff and coordination overhead. She does not quantify total time saved or accuracy. This applies to legal-industry analysis rather than demonstrating autonomous legal practice.

pts.k: Um claims meaningful AI adoption costs extend beyond software purchases to scarce lawyer time, integration, experimentation, and workflow change.
pts.d: Um reports hearing that some firms spend up to 2% of revenue on AI, without identifying those firms or providing a cost breakdown. She argues that lawyer time is perishable inventory, so time devoted to changing behavior is a real investment cost. This is a current adoption claim in the 2026 interview, affecting firms' investment capacity and lawyers' allocation of time; the reported percentage is not presented as an industry average.

pts.k: Um expects law firms' AI deployments to differ according to their competitive positioning, client base, and work rather than converge on a single strategy.
pts.d: Um supports this argument with selected firm examples: Kirkland and Cooley investing without public disclosure; HSF Kramer embedding technical capability through a forward-deployed engineer model suited to disputes and arbitration; and A&O Shearman building on application-layer experience and financial-institution relationships. These are examples of strategic fit, not demonstrated comparative returns. She explicitly says it is too early to grade the investment theses.

pts.k: Um predicts that allocating junior-lawyer time to AI learning will generate returns, help discover scalable applications, and differentiate firms in recruiting.
pts.d: Responding to the example of Ropes & Gray crediting AI experimentation toward associate targets, Um endorses the approach and connects it to her earlier proposal for intensive AI training of first-year associates. Her rationale is that first-years are not yet the most productive lawyers and that learning requires immersion. The return on investment and recruitment benefits are her expectations, not measured outcomes. She also discusses potential entry into middle-market work, but that particular possibility is relayed from a firm leader rather than independently established.

pts.k: Um argues that clarity about client value equips law firm leaders to navigate AI, while distance from clients makes its effects harder to understand.
pts.d: Based on her conversations with managing partners, Um contrasts leaders grounded in what they sell and why clients buy with those who are less confident in their value proposition. She says talent leadership remains important but must be combined with partners' understanding of client realities. Her statement that leaders must address AI by the end of 2026 is a normative deadline, not an empirically established market tipping point.

pts.k: Um predicts that AI-enabled alternatives can cause law firm work and revenue to disappear without an observable fee negotiation or explicit client warning.
pts.d: Um develops this scenario from anonymous early-adopter corporate-counsel accounts included in her rankings article. Her own claim is that clients may substitute much cheaper ways of doing work, leaving the former provider unaware of the lost opportunity. She explicitly cautions that these clients are not representative of most buyers and that this is not a clear and imminent disaster. The transcript offers no representative estimate of how much work has shifted.

pts.k: Um identifies distributed, intermittent, price-sensitive work as especially vulnerable to rapid substitution with weak warning signals.
pts.d: Her argument distinguishes major strategic accounts, where trusted partner relationships can reveal changing client expectations, from similar work delivered across many clients without ongoing relationships. In the latter market, she predicts that a new offering can diffuse quickly while early signals remain invisible to incumbent firms. This is a conditional strategic assessment, not a measured adoption forecast. She recommends closer monitoring where price is a significant selection factor and firms cannot clearly establish differentiated capability.

pts.k: Um predicts both AI-enhanced boutiques and 'bionic insourcing,' with insourcing potentially transforming corporate legal work more fundamentally than AI transforms boutique firms.
pts.d: Um argues that some work currently sent to law firms or ALSPs would be better performed inside companies because it needs integration with business processes or rapid application of legal judgment close to the business. She also cautions that some historically insourced work should have remained with providers, so this is not a blanket endorsement of insourcing. The prediction has no specified completion date and is based on her interpretation of work allocation and emerging AI possibilities, not a quantified study. ALSPs here are providers of legal work, distinct from software vendors.

pts.k: Um predicts that AI disruption will often appear as gradually intensifying commercial pressure rather than clearly identifiable AI-caused failure.
pts.d: Building on an anonymous client's demand that providers eliminate inefficient billable hours, Um describes harder business development, fewer new matters, resistance to rates, and declining realization. These are her projected mechanisms, not measured AI-attributable changes in the rankings data. She says she advanced this framing to managing partners three years before the interview and reiterates it in 2026, without specifying when each effect will occur.

pts.k: Um predicts consolidation, refragmentation, and new challengers rather than either unchanged incumbent survival or the disappearance of the legal profession.
pts.d: Um estimates that roughly 300 consequential global law firms serve enterprise clients and are intended to outlast their name partners, and doubts there is room for the current set because not all management teams can navigate the transition. She anticipates competition among industrial-scale incumbents alongside pressure from substitutes and names Norm AI and General Legal as examples of emerging challengers. Venture-capital and private-equity investment is part of her rationale, but she supplies no survival model, quantified failure forecast, or fixed horizon. The '300' is her approximate market characterization, not an AI-displacement statistic.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The AI claims rest mainly on Um's firsthand experience, firm examples, professional conversations, anonymous early-adopter accounts, and strategic inference.
pts.d: Um describes a quantitative rankings process based on ALM firm financial and headcount information, supplemented by qualitative research. However, she does not present those rankings as a causal measurement of AI's effects on revenue, profit, employment, or market concentration. Her analytical-workflow account is experiential; the spending figure is reported from firms; training returns and market restructuring are predictions. The anonymous client accounts illustrate possible mechanisms rather than establish prevalence. The Big Tech capital-expenditure and McKinsey adoption figures raised by a host are not independent findings advanced by Um in this interview.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Um distinguishes present adoption experience from early-stage investment assessments and undated disruption scenarios.
pts.d: The workflow and investment observations concern the 2026 interview period, with explicit comparisons to the previous year. She gives the end of 2026 as a deadline for leadership communication, not for universal adoption or displacement. Investment returns, substitution, bionic insourcing, and market restructuring have no precise horizon. Adoption depends on preparation, workflow integration, time for learning, client needs, and firm positioning. She expressly limits the generalizability and immediacy of the early-adopter buyer signals.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The predicted effects are differentiated across enterprise-facing firms, associates, firm leaders, corporate legal departments, ALSPs, and new competitors.
pts.d: Associates face investment in new ways of practicing, and students may use AI training support to distinguish employers. Partners and firm leaders face investment choices, pressure on matters and pricing, and a need for closer client intelligence. Corporate legal departments may bring work inside and redesign its relationship to business processes. Law firms and ALSPs may lose work better performed internally. Firms serving intermittent, price-sensitive demand face greater silent-substitution risk than firms with strong strategic-account relationships. Boutique firms may become more capable, while large incumbents may consolidate or be displaced by challengers. The discussion does not supply a concrete forecast of lawyer job losses or claims about access to justice for underserved individuals.
